title: No. 17 — The Same Subject Continued (The Insufficiency of the Present Confederation to Preserve the Union) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: An objection different from the one stated and answered in my last paper may also be urged against the principle of legislating for individual citizens of America. It may be said that this would tend to make the government of the Union too powerful and to enable it to absorb those residual authorities that ought to be left with the States for local purposes. Granting the love of power its widest reasonable scope, I confess I am at a loss to see what temptation those entrusted with the administration of the general government could ever feel to strip the States of authorities of that kind. The regulation of the merely domestic affairs of a State seems to me to offer little allurement to ambition. Commerce, finance, negotiation, and war seem to take in all the objects that have charms for minds governed by that passion, and all the powers necessary for those objects ought, in the first instance, to be lodged in the national depository. The administration of private justice between citizens of the same State, the supervision of agriculture and similar concerns—in short, all the matters proper for local legislation—can never be desirable charges of a general jurisdiction. It is therefore unlikely that the federal councils would be inclined to usurp such powers. The attempt to exercise them would be as troublesome as it would be useless, and the possession of them would for that reason add nothing to the dignity, importance, or splendor of the national government.

But suppose, for argument's sake, that mere wantonness and lust of domination would be enough to produce that disposition. Even then it can be safely affirmed that the sense of the constituent body of the national representatives—in other words, the people of the several States—would check the indulgence of so extravagant an appetite. It will always be far easier for the State governments to encroach on the national authorities than for the national government to encroach on the State authorities. The proof of this turns on the greater degree of influence the State governments will generally have over the people, provided they administer their affairs with uprightness and prudence. This same fact also teaches us that there is an inherent and intrinsic weakness in all federal constitutions, and that no pains can be too great in their organization to give them all the force compatible with the principles of liberty.

The superior influence of the particular governments would result partly from the diffuse construction of the national government, but mainly from the nature of the objects to which the State administrations would devote their attention.

It is a known fact about human nature that its affections are commonly weaker the more distant or diffuse the object. By the same principle that a man is more attached to his family than to his neighborhood, and to his neighborhood than to the community at large, the people of each State would tend to feel a stronger bias toward their local governments than toward the government of the Union—unless the force of that principle were destroyed by a much better administration of the latter.
This strong inclination of the human heart would find powerful reinforcements in the objects of State regulation.

The variety of more minute interests that will necessarily fall under the supervision of the local administrations, and which will form so many small streams of influence running through every part of society, cannot be specified without involving a level of detail too tedious and uninteresting to be worth the instruction it might give.

There is one transcendent advantage belonging to the province of the State governments, and it alone is enough to settle the matter clearly: I mean the ordinary administration of criminal and civil justice. This, more than anything else, is the most powerful, most universal, and most attractive source of popular obedience and attachment. As the immediate and visible guardian of life and property—its benefits and its terrors constantly active before the public eye, regulating all those personal interests and familiar concerns to which individual sensitivity is most awake—it does more than any other circumstance to imprint on the people's minds affection, esteem, and reverence toward the government. This great cement of society, which will spread almost wholly through the channels of the particular governments, would by itself give them so decisive a hold over their respective citizens as to make them at all times a complete counterweight—and, not infrequently, a dangerous rival—to the power of the Union.

The operations of the national government, on the other hand, fall less immediately under the observation of the mass of citizens. The benefits derived from it will mainly be perceived and attended to by speculative thinkers. Relating to more general interests, they will be less likely to come home to the feelings of the people, and so less likely to inspire a habitual sense of obligation and an active sentiment of attachment.
The reasoning here has been abundantly illustrated by the experience of all federal constitutions we are acquainted with, and of all others that have borne the slightest analogy to them.

Although the ancient feudal systems were not, strictly speaking, confederacies, they shared the nature of that kind of association. There was a common head, chieftain, or sovereign whose authority extended over the whole nation, and a number of subordinate vassals, or feudatories, who held large portions of land allotted to them and had numerous trains of INFERIOR vassals or retainers who occupied and cultivated that land on terms of fealty or obedience to the persons who held it. Each principal vassal was a kind of sovereign within his particular domain. The consequences were a continual opposition to the authority of the sovereign and frequent wars between the great barons or chief feudatories themselves. The power of the head of the nation was usually too weak either to keep the public peace or to protect the people from the oppression of their immediate lords. This period of European history is emphatically called by historians the times of feudal anarchy.

When the sovereign happened to be a man of vigorous and warlike temper and superior abilities, he would acquire a personal weight and influence that served, for the time, the purpose of a more regular authority. But in general the power of the barons triumphed over that of the prince. In many instances his rule was thrown off entirely, and the great fiefs were erected into independent principalities or States. In those cases where the monarch finally prevailed over his vassals, his success owed mainly to the tyranny of those vassals over their dependents. The barons, or nobles, equally the enemies of the sovereign and the oppressors of the common people, were dreaded and detested by both, until mutual danger and mutual interest produced a union between them fatal to the power of the aristocracy. Had the nobles, by clemency and justice, kept the loyalty and devotion of their retainers and followers, the contests between them and the prince would almost always have ended in their favor, and in the curtailment or overthrow of the royal authority.

This is no mere speculation or conjecture. Among the many illustrations of its truth that could be cited, Scotland furnishes a powerful example. The spirit of clanship, introduced early into that kingdom and uniting the nobles and their dependents by ties equivalent to kinship, made the aristocracy a constant overmatch for the power of the monarch—until the union with England subdued its fierce and ungovernable spirit and reduced it within those rules of subordination that a more rational and energetic system of civil polity had previously established in the latter kingdom.

The separate governments in a confederacy may aptly be compared to the feudal baronies, with this advantage in their favor: from the reasons already explained, they will generally have the confidence and goodwill of the people, and with such important support they will be able to oppose effectively all encroachments by the national government. We will be fortunate if they are not able to thwart its legitimate and necessary authority. The points of similarity lie in the rivalry of power applicable to both, and in the CONCENTRATION of large portions of the strength of the community into particular DEPOSITORIES—in one case at the disposal of individuals, in the other at the disposal of political bodies.

A brief review of the events that have attended confederate governments will further illustrate this important doctrine. Inattention to it has been the great source of our political mistakes and has misdirected our jealousy to the wrong side. This review will be the subject of some upcoming papers.
